The reader should notice how small the demand is. A people who had crossed a sea and drunk from a rock are being asked for one beast, and the asking is where the trouble starts. Nothing in the instruction requires interpretation, and nothing in it is beyond their means.

## The suspicion

Their reply is not a question about which cow. It is a question about whether the man is serious.

That is a remarkable thing to say to a prophet, and the surah records it without softening. A people who suspect mockery in a plain command have already decided something about the one giving it, and that decision precedes the instruction and survives every answer it receives.

## The defence

Moses answers with a refuge from foolishness. He does not argue and he does not explain, and he places himself outside the accusation by appealing to the one who sent him rather than by defending himself.

The phrase he uses names the charge as foolishness, and it is the only word of rebuke in the exchange. He is more alarmed at the suggestion that he would play with a command than at their refusal to comply.

## Why the story starts here

Everything that follows depends on this moment. The questioning that fills the next four verses is not curiosity but the continuation of a suspicion, and the suspicion is answered by being given exactly what it asked for, one detail at a time.

The surah will show the people narrowing their own instruction until the animal is nearly impossible to find. That process starts with a man being asked whether he is joking.

## In short

- The command is short, specific, and modest, which makes the reaction the subject of the verse.
- Their question is about the messenger's seriousness rather than the instruction's content.
- Moses answers with a refuge rather than an argument, and the rebuke lands on the suggestion of foolishness.
- The narrowing of the command over the next four verses grows out of this first suspicion.

## What the verse does

==They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!” He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded!’”== grants the first request and returns the same instruction at the end.

## Asking for detail

The demand is framed as a request for clarity. On the surface it is reasonable. A command to sacrifice a cow could be satisfied by any cow, and they want to know that they are doing it right.

The wording gives them away. They ask Moses to call upon his Lord, as though the Lord were his and not theirs, and the phrase puts a small distance between the people and the one commanding them. A people who do not own the command will not hurry to keep it.

## The answer given

The reply narrows the animal and then repeats the original instruction word for word. Neither too old nor too young, but in between.

That answer is generous and it is also a rebuke. They asked for a description and were given one, and the description is followed by the same command they had already received.

## The repetition

The final clause is the important one. So do as you are commanded. The verse has answered their question and has not moved an inch from where it started.

A reader can hear the patience in it. The instruction has been restated rather than replaced, and the restating says that the first version was sufficient. It is the answer a teacher gives to a pupil who has asked a question already covered.

## What the request cost

The animal is now specified where it had been open. They had a whole herd to choose from and they have narrowed it to a particular age, and the narrowing was their own doing.

That is the pattern the next three verses will repeat. Each question buys a detail and pays for it with a smaller range of options, and the surah records the transaction without comment, leaving the reader to see the price.

## In short

- The request for clarity is reasonable on its surface and revealing in its wording.
- The answer specifies an age and then repeats the original command unchanged.
- The repetition is patient rather than sharp, and it says that the first instruction was enough.
- Each question narrows the animal, so the people are paying for the detail with their own options.

## What the verse does

==They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see.’”== is the second exchange in the same pattern, and the detail added is a colour.

## The same request again

The wording of the question is almost identical to the previous verse. They ask Moses to call upon his Lord and to specify a further feature, and the near repetition is itself part of the record.

The repetition is the story. A second question that adds nothing new to the situation is no longer a request for information but a way of staying in the conversation without moving, and the verse records the phrasing as carefully as the content.

## What is added

The colour is specified as a bright yellow, and the verse adds a phrase going beyond the question. The animal is pleasant to look at, which the question had not asked for.

That phrase is the interesting part. Nobody asked about beauty and the answer supplies it, describing the command in terms that appeal to the eye. It is a strange generosity in a story about reluctance.

## Why the detail matters

A yellow cow is easy to find. A yellow cow that is pleasant to look at is easier still, because any healthy animal in good condition will do, and a herd in that country would hold several.

So the specification is not a trap. The animal is narrowed in a way that still leaves a broad field, and the people are the ones narrowing it further with each request.

## The cost again

By this point they have asked twice and received two descriptions. They are further from the deed than at the start, and every answer has left them with more to check.

The surah does not say this in a sentence. It lets the reader add up the verses and feel the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is the lesson it wants him to learn.

## In short

- The second question repeats the first almost word for word, which shows it is about delay rather than information.
- The answer adds beauty to colour, a detail nobody asked for and a sign of generosity.
- The specification still leaves a broad field, so the narrowing is coming from the people rather than the command.
- Two answers have moved them further from the deed, and the reader is left to do the arithmetic.

## What the verse does

==Again they said, “Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow, for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.”== is the third request, and this one finally contains a reason.

## The excuse offered

They explain the question by saying that cows look alike. That is true of cows and it is not a reason to ask a prophet a third time, and the verse lets the weakness of the excuse stand.

The verse records the excuse without evaluating it. The reader has watched two specifications arrive and can judge for himself whether the field is still confusing, and the judgement is the point of the silence.

## The first sign of softening

Then they add a phrase that has not appeared before. If Allah wills. It is a small acknowledgement that the matter is not in their hands, and after two verses of treating it as entirely theirs it arrives almost as a surprise.

The surah places the phrase in the mouths of people who have spent two verses treating the matter as entirely in their hands. The contrast is quiet and it is the only movement in the passage, and it is easy to miss because it is only three words.

## Why the phrase matters

A person who says that God willing has admitted that the outcome is not his to control, whatever else he thinks and however little he has changed.

The verse does not reward the admission immediately, and the next verse makes the command harder again. But the admission has been made, and the surah records it in the middle of a stubborn passage.

## A promise, at last

They also promise to be guided if the answer comes. That is the first commitment anyone in this story has offered, and it appears only after the third request, which tells the reader how commitments of that kind are produced.

The reader should notice what produced it. Not the command and not the first two answers, but the experience of asking repeatedly and getting no nearer the act.

## In short

- The excuse is true and irrelevant, and the verse records it without comment.
- The phrase if Allah wills is the first admission in the story that the matter is not in their hands.
- The admission is not rewarded at once, since the next verse narrows the command again.
- The first promise to obey appears only after three requests, and the reader is meant to notice what produced it.

## What the verse does

==He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish.’” They said, “Now you have come with the truth.” Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly== ends the questioning, narrows the animal to its final form, and records a slaughter that was almost missed.

## The final description

The animal must not be one that has been worked. It has not pulled a plough and it has not carried water, and it is sound and unmarked, which in that setting describes a beast kept for breeding or for milk.

The specification is complete, describing an animal valuable to its owner. A beast that has never worked is not the cheap option, and the command has moved far from verse 67.

## The owner's cost

That detail is where the passage has been heading. A cow that does not work is one somebody kept for something better.

The narrowing came from the questions, and it has landed on a neighbour. The cost of the delay falls on a person who never spoke.

## The concession

Then they say that the truth has come. After three requests and a final description, they accept what they were told at the beginning, and the acceptance is worded as though the truth had only now arrived.

The verse records the concession plainly and does not celebrate it. It arrives four verses late, because the alternatives have run out.

## The hesitation

The last clause is the one that stays. They slaughtered it, and they nearly did not.

That word converts obedience into something barely distinguishable from it, a deed performed under protest that has not become a turn.

## Why the story ends here

The rest of the story reveals what the cow was for, and the answer is shocking. But the surah pauses on the hesitation, because hesitation is what this people keeps producing.

Every gift in the passage met the same reflex. They are not a people who refuse but one that arrives late, asks too much, and complies with its hands while its heart is elsewhere.

## In short

- The final description names an expensive animal, and the command has travelled far from the plain instruction of verse 67.
- The cost of the delay falls on an owner who never spoke, which is where the passage has been heading.
- The concession arrives four verses late and the verse does not celebrate it.
- One word about hesitation converts the obedience into something that is barely a turn, and that reflex is what this people repeatedly produces.

## What the verse does

==˹This is˺ when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed== finally explains why a cow was demanded, and the explanation turns the story from a test of obedience into a murder inquiry.

## The crime behind the command

A man was killed and the community argued about who did it. The verse does not say they were confused but that they disputed, which suggests positions were being defended and reputations protected, and a community in that state is not looking for an answer to anything.

A people unable to agree on a killer, with no witness and no evidence, had a problem no argument could settle, and the command they avoided for four verses was the answer to it, offered in the plainest form available.

## The concealment

Then the verse says the concealment was revealed. The word is the one used earlier of people who hid what they knew, linking this killing to the whole record.

That clause changes the temperature. The questioning about the cow was not the main sin of the passage but a small visible instance of something larger underneath, and the verse lets the reader work out the scale of it.

## What the reader now knows

Everything is reframed. The reluctance was not caution but the behaviour of people with something to hide, and the four verses of questioning take on the shape of people who would rather talk than act, because acting might reveal something.

The reader is invited back over those verses with different eyes, and what looked like slowness reads as protection, and what looked like caution reads as concealment.

## Why the story is told in this order

The surah could have begun with the murder, then the command, and that order would have been clearer and far less effective.

The order chosen makes the reader feel the reluctance first and the reason second, trusting him to hold two pieces until they fit.

## In short

- The command was the answer to a real problem, a killing that no argument could settle.
- The concealment mentioned at the end reframes the whole story, since the questioning was an instance of something larger.
- Read again, the previous four verses become the movements of people with something to hide.
- Telling the reluctance before the reason makes the reader experience the evasion before he understands it.

## What the verse does

==So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.” This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs so that you may understand== delivers the purpose of the command and turns a local story into a statement about resurrection.

## The instruction

A piece of the sacrificed animal is to be struck against the body. The act is strange and physical, and the verse gives it without any explanation of the mechanism.

What the reader is meant to notice is that the cow does nothing. It is a piece of meat, and the account does not pretend otherwise. The animal is a means and the verse treats it as one.

## What it demonstrates

Then the verse names the point of the whole episode. This is how the dead are brought back.

The demonstration is not an argument for resurrection but an instance of it, performed in front of witnesses on a body they could see. It is evidence of a kind this people had been given several times and had already failed to absorb.

## The word easily

A small phrase in the line does real work. The raising is described as easy, and the word is a comparison rather than a claim about effort.

The comparison is against the objections a person carries about distance and decay. The verse answers none of them, reducing the whole matter to something struck with a piece of meat.

## Why signs are given

The verse ends by saying these signs were shown so that they might understand. The purpose is comprehension rather than belief.

That distinction is the tragedy of the passage. These people were given evidence designed to produce understanding, and they produced questions about the age and colour of a cow.

## What the reader takes

The reader has seen the same pattern in his own reading. He has been shown a sea, a rock, and now a resurrection, and the response being described is one he can recognise.

The verse does not condemn him for it. It shows him the pattern clearly, in a people he is not, and leaves the recognition to do its work.

## In short

- The animal is a means and the verse treats it as one, and nothing about its action is explained.
- The demonstration is an instance rather than an argument, shown on a body the witnesses could see.
- The word easily reduces the objections without answering them, which is the surah's method throughout.
- The verse names understanding as the purpose, and the gap between that purpose and the people's questions is the tragedy.

## What the verse does

==Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah. And Allah is never unaware of what you do== follows a resurrection with a description of stone, and the comparison is not flattering to the stones.

## After the sign

The verse opens with a phrase measuring the distance from the miracle. Even after that, the hearts hardened, and no reason is given because the reason is the whole passage.

The placement is the accusation. A dead man stood up and identified his killer, and the effect was stone.

## A comparison that goes wrong for the people

The obvious image would be a heart like a rock, and the verse begins there, then improves on it in the wrong direction and calls the hearts harder.

What follows explains why. Rocks are not uniformly dead. Some produce water, some break apart, some respond.

## Three rocks

The three examples come from things this passage has shown. A rock produced twelve springs, and a mountain broke when glory touched it.

So the comparison is not abstract. The reader has watched stone behave better than the people it is describing.

## What a hard heart is

In this book a hard heart is not one without feeling but one that does not respond to what it has been shown.

That definition makes the condition diagnosable. A person can be moved to tears and still have a heart of stone.

## The closing assurance

The verse ends by saying Allah is not unaware of what they do. The plainness is the point, since they had acted as though a matter could be kept out of sight.

The verse closes by naming what they had forgotten, and it does so without anger.

## Why the first part ends here

This ends the first long movement about this people, which ran from verse 40 and ends on stone. What follows changes tone, and the reader has been given much evidence of a community's failure.

## In short

- The phrase even then places the hardening after a resurrection, and the placement is the accusation.
- The comparison improves in the wrong direction, since rock turns out to be the more responsive material.
- The three rocks are things the people have already seen, so the comparison is evidence rather than image.
- A hard heart is one that does not respond to what it is shown, and the passage ends by naming the one thing the people had forgotten.

## What the verse does

==Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you, though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it== turns from the people to the reader who is still hoping something of them.

## A question to the hopeful

The verse is addressed to believers, and the question is about expectation rather than conduct. It asks whether the hope is reasonable, not whether it is generous, and the distinction is important because the readers being questioned were not being accused of anything.

The previous verse had described hearts harder than stone. A reader could have concluded that the situation was difficult and that effort might still work. This line removes that conclusion by asking him to look at what has already been tried.

## The charge in the middle

Then comes the accusation, and it is specific. A group of them heard the word of Allah and then altered it, deliberately, after they had understood it.

The two adverbs carry the weight. Knowingly excludes error. After understanding excludes ignorance. What is described is not a people who failed to grasp a message but a people who grasped it and then changed it.

## Why understanding makes it worse

A person who mishears a message can be corrected by hearing it again. A person who understands and alters it has already been given the only remedy available, and the verse does not suggest a second one exists.

The verse makes this the ground of the question. Expectation is unreasonable not because the people are hopeless by nature but because the specific thing hoped for has already been refused, with full knowledge.

## What the verse does not say

It does not say every one of them did this. It says a group. The verse is precise about the size of the accusation, the precision is a form of fairness, and a reader who wants to read it as a verdict on a whole people is stopped by a single word.

So the reader is not being told to write off a people. He is told to stop expecting fidelity from a group whose record is already established, and to place his hope where the text places it.

## In short

- The question is about the reasonableness of hope rather than the goodness of the reader.
- The charge is specific, and knowingly and after understanding remove both error and ignorance.
- Understanding makes the alteration worse, since it was the only remedy available.
- The verse says a group, not all of them, and the precision keeps the accusation fair.

## What the verse does

==When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?”== returns to a scene the surah has already staged once and shows it with the words included.

## The same two rooms

Verse 14 recorded a group saying one thing in public and another in private. This verse does the same, with one difference. Here the reader is given the content of the private conversation, and being let in on the argument changes what the scene means.

That difference matters. In the earlier passage the reader watched the mockery. Here he watches a debate about tactics, and the debate is about what should be disclosed.

## The public word

They say they believe, and the statement is brief. The brevity is consistent with everything the surah has said about this group. The public sentence is short because it is a transaction rather than a conviction, and the verse does not pause over it. It moves at once to the room where the real conversation happens.

## The private argument

Inside, the question is whether to tell the believers what has been disclosed to them. The reasoning is that the believers will use it as evidence against them.

So the truth is being treated as material that could be used in a dispute. The people in the room are not asking whether something is true but who benefits if it becomes known, and the second question has replaced the first entirely.

## The rebuke inside the question

The last clause asks whether they do not understand, and it is aimed at their own reasoning. The verse is saying that the calculation does not work.

A person who conceals what he knows from the one who revealed it has not protected himself. The verse lets the reader see how clever the reasoning sounds from inside the room and how small it looks from outside, and the gap between those two views is the whole verse.

## In short

- The verse revisits the two rooms of verse 14 and this time gives the private words.
- The public statement is short because it is a transaction rather than a conviction.
- The private debate treats truth as evidence in a dispute rather than as something to be answered.
- The closing question turns their own cleverness against them, since the calculation does not work.

## What the verse does

==Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal== is the shortest verse in this stretch and it answers the private conversation with a single fact.

## One sentence

The verse does not explain, argue, or develop. It states that the concealment and the disclosure are both known, and it stops.

That brevity is the form of the answer. A private conversation had been held on the assumption that it was private, and the verse says the assumption was wrong, and does so in a single clause without raising its voice.

## The two verbs again

Concealing and revealing have been paired before in this surah, at the end of the scene with the angels. There the pair described the scope of knowledge. Here it describes the scope of a single question.

The repetition is deliberate. The reader has been told once that nothing is hidden. The verse reminds him at the exact point where a group is behaving as though something is, and it chooses that moment rather than the opening of the story.

## The question form

The verse asks whether they know, and the asking is not a request for information. It is the tone of a person pointing at something obvious that has been overlooked.

That tone is a mercy as well as a rebuke. A fact stated flatly would close a door. A question leaves the hearer room to answer differently, and the verse offers that room in the middle of a hard passage, where a reader might have expected none.

## What it does to the scene

The private conversation has just been recorded. The verse does not comment on it and does not judge it. It simply places a fact next to it and lets the two sit together, since a fact placed beside a scene is often louder than a verdict pronounced over it.

The reader supplies the conclusion. That is how much of this surah works, and this verse is one of the shortest and cleanest examples of the method.

## In short

- One fact is stated and nothing is argued, and the brevity is the form of the answer.
- The pair of verbs echoes the scene with the angels, where the same pair described the scope of knowledge.
- The question form leaves the hearer room to answer differently rather than closing a door.
- The conclusion is left to the reader, which is how much of this surah works.

## What the verse does

==And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate== turns from the scholars to the ordinary people and describes what they have been given.

## A group without access

The verse names a group who cannot read the book, and it does not blame them for that. The word describes an absence of learning rather than a moral failing.

What it does blame is what has filled the space. They know nothing except lies, and the lies were not their own composition. They received them from people who could read, and the verse is careful about where the contents came from.

## What they were handed

A people who cannot check a text must rely on whoever reads it to them. The verse says what arrived through that channel, and the arrival is the subject.

The line therefore sits directly after the scholars and before the woe that follows. The reader is being shown a chain, and the link between the two groups is what the chain is made of.

## Wishes instead of knowledge

The last word describes a state of guessing from desire, believing something because it is agreeable rather than because it has been established, and a person in that state has no way of telling the two apart.

That is the condition of a person with no access to the source and a strong interest in the outcome, and the verse presents it as the predictable result of the arrangement just described rather than as a personal failing.

## Where the blame falls

The verse places the ordinary people in a chain and the scholars at the other end. Both are described, and the description of the second group is much harsher.

The reader should notice the fairness in this. The people who could not read are described as misled. The people who did the misleading are the subject of the next verse, and the difference in tone between the two is the surah's judgement.

## In short

- The group is described by an absence of learning rather than by a fault, and the blame falls on what filled the space.
- A people unable to check a text depend on whoever reads to them, and the verse names what arrived through that channel.
- Guessing from desire is presented as the predictable result of the arrangement, not as innocence.
- The verse describes the misled before it describes the misleaders, and the difference in tone is the judgement.

## What the verse does

==So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned== is the sharpest verse in this passage, and it pronounces woe twice.

## The act

The charge is writing with their own hands and then attributing the writing to Allah. The verse does not say they misread or misremembered. It describes production.

The phrase with their own hands is doing the work. The thing that was claimed to come from elsewhere has fingerprints on it, and the fingerprints belong to the people making the claim.

## The double woe

Woe is pronounced once for what the hands wrote and once for what they earned. The repetition separates the act from its profit, and both are condemned.

That separation is important. A reader might think the offence ends with the document. The second woe says the gain that motivated the document is also part of it.

## The motive named

The verse names the reason in a phrase, and the phrase means something small and passing. They did it for a price.

The smallness is the accusation. What was traded was enormous and what was received was not, and the verse lets the disproportion sit in a single word rather than spelling it out.

## Why the verse is placed here

The chain from the previous verse now has its beginning. Ordinary people were fed lies, and this verse names the people producing them.

The passage has been moving steadily from the crowd to the source, and this is the furthest point of that movement. Everything after it will deal with the consequences rather than the cause.

## What it does to the reader

The verse is aimed at people who handle a text, and every reader of this book is in that category by the act of reading.

That is not an accident of placement. The surah has been careful throughout to keep its accusations available to the person holding it, and this verse is one of the clearest instances of that care.

## In short

- The charge is production rather than error, and the phrase with their own hands is the evidence.
- Woe is pronounced twice, separating the act from the profit that motivated it.
- The motive is named as something small and passing, and the disproportion does the accusing.
- The passage has moved from crowd to source, and the verse leaves every reader who handles a text inside its reach.

## What the verse does

==˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah—for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?”== takes a claim about being spared and answers it with a question about paperwork.

## The claim

The statement is that the fire will touch them only briefly. The number is not given, and the vagueness suits a claim that was never argued for.

What is really being asserted is an exemption, and an exemption needs a source. That is the weak point, and the verse goes straight to it.

## The question

The reply asks whether a pledge was taken from Allah. The wording is chosen with care, because a pledge from Allah would be binding and Allah does not break His word.

So the question is not rhetorical in the ordinary sense. It grants the possibility and asks for the document, and there is no document.

## The alternative offered

The verse then supplies the other explanation. If no pledge exists, the claim is simply something being said about Allah without knowledge.

That is the more serious charge of the two, and the verse puts it second. A person can be wrong about a promise. A person who invents one has done something else.

## Who is asked to say this

The instruction is given to the messenger, and he is told to put the question to them. The verse is therefore a script for a conversation rather than a verdict delivered from a distance.

That form leaves the hearer room. The claim can be examined and abandoned, and the question is asked in a way that makes abandoning it possible.

## What kind of confidence this is

The verse is willing to be settled by evidence. Send for the pledge, and if it exists the claim stands.

That is the same confidence shown in the challenge to produce a surah. The surah repeatedly invites inspection, and this verse does so in a matter the claimants could have settled with a single document.

## In short

- The claim asserts an exemption, and an exemption needs a source.
- The question about a pledge is not rhetorical, since a pledge from Allah would settle the matter.
- The alternative charge is heavier, because inventing a promise is different from being wrong about one.
- The verse is a script for a conversation and it invites settlement by evidence, which is the surah's confidence throughout.

## What the verse does

==But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever== rejects the claim of the previous verse and replaces the exemption with a rule.

## The word that opens it

The verse begins with a particle of correction, close in force to a flat denial. It does not argue with the claim. It sets it aside.

That abruptness is the tone the passage has been building toward. The claim of a short stay has been examined and found to lack a document, and the verse does not spend more time on it.

## What the condition describes

The two clauses describe someone who does wrong and then remains in it. The second clause carries the sense of being wrapped up in the wrong, surrounded by it on every side.

So the verse is not describing a person who fell once. It is describing a person whose falling has become his situation, and the distinction is the same one drawn at verse 7 about people who persist.

## What is earned

The word used for the wrong is one that carries the idea of acquiring, of bringing something into one's own possession. The image behind it is a trade rather than an accident.

A person who earns has gained something he now owns. The verse is saying that wrong done repeatedly becomes property, and property is not shed easily.

## The rule stated

Then the sentence gives the outcome without qualification. The residents of the fire, permanently.

The surah has used the same construction for the other outcome in the next verse. The two are deliberately matched, so that the reader sees one rule applied in two directions rather than two separate decrees.

## Why the flatness works

The verse offers no comfort and no narrowing. After a passage full of argument, the plainness lands harder than another question would.

The next verse supplies the other half of the pair. Placing the two side by side means the reader cannot take one without seeing the shape of the whole arrangement.

## In short

- The verse opens with a flat denial rather than an argument, and the abruptness is the tone.
- The condition describes someone wrapped up in wrong rather than someone who fell once.
- The language of earning presents repeated wrong as property, and property is not shed easily.
- The rule is stated plainly because it is one half of a pair, and the next verse gives the other.

## What the verse does

==And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever== completes the pair begun in the previous verse, and the two sentences are built to match.

## The same shape

The structure is identical. A condition, a residence, a permanence. The verse does not soften the symmetry by adding explanation to one side, and the plainness of the pairing is more persuasive than any comment would be.

That symmetry is the point. A reader who has just heard a hard rule is shown the same rule running in the other direction, with the same words doing the same work, and the arrangement makes the two outcomes two halves of one account.

## Two conditions

Belief is named and is not left alone. Doing good is attached to it, and the attachment is the surah's persistent concern. The pairing has appeared repeatedly, and each time the same distinction is made. A claim is not a state, and the verse refuses to count belief without the action that would follow it.

## The same residence

Both groups are called residents, and the word is the one used of the fire. What differs is the place and not the kind of tenure.

The verse is telling the reader that permanence is not a reward added to a pleasant outcome but a property of the outcome itself, and both destinations share it.

## What the pairing achieves

The reader has been given an exemption that did not hold and a rule that did. Setting the two outcomes together means the rule is not a threat aimed at one people but a description of how the matter works, and a description is harder to dismiss than a threat.

That description has been the method since verse 2. The surah has shown portraits, made arguments, and offered challenges, and here it states the two destinations and leaves the reader with them.

## In short

- The two verses are built to match, and the symmetry is the point rather than an accident of style.
- Belief is named with doing good attached, which is the surah's persistent distinction between claim and state.
- Both destinations share the word for residence, so permanence is a property of the outcome rather than a reward.
- The pairing turns the rule from a threat aimed at one people into a description of how the matter works.

## What the verse does

==And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.” But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent== sets out the terms of the agreement in a list, and the list is almost entirely about how people treat one another.

## What the covenant contained

The first item is worship of one, and it is stated as the ground of everything after it. The remaining five are obligations between people.

That proportion is worth noticing. One item concerns the divine and five concern neighbours, and the five include the two that the surah has already named as marks of the believers.

## A widening circle

The list of people moves outward. Parents first, then relatives, then orphans and the needy, and then everyone else in the phrase about speaking kindly.

The order goes from those with the strongest claim on a person to those with none except their need. A reader who stops at the family has not yet reached the end of the instruction.

## The two practices

Prayer and alms are the familiar pair, and they appear in the middle of the list rather than at its head. They have been named before as marks of the guided and will be named again.

Their position suggests they are part of a single fabric rather than separate items. A covenant that includes worship, family, the poor, speech, prayer, and giving is a description of a whole life rather than a set of duties.

## The response

Then the verse turns and reports what happened. They turned away, all but a few, and were indifferent.

The word indifference is the last nail. Not opposition, not argument. A people who simply did not care, and the verse names that as the response to a covenant that had been set out this clearly.

## In short

- One item concerns worship and five concern how people treat one another, and the proportion is deliberate.
- The list widens from parents to the needy to everyone, so a reader who stops at family has not finished.
- Prayer and alms sit inside the fabric rather than at its head, which makes the covenant a whole life.
- The response named is indifference rather than opposition, and that is the last nail in the verse.

## What the verse does

==And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness== states a second covenant and then fixes the responsibility with two words.

## A narrower agreement

The first covenant concerned worship, family, and the poor. This one concerns two things only, and both are about the harm a community can do to itself, which makes it the more specific and the more personal of the two.

Blood and homes. A person can lose his life or lose his place, and the verse names the two as the things the agreement protected.

## The unusual wording

The instruction is worded as though the people were being told not to kill themselves and not to expel themselves. That phrasing is not a slip, and the verse uses it twice in the same sentence.

It treats the community as a single body. A member killed is a wound in the whole, and a family driven out is the whole expelling part of itself, and the covenant was made on that understanding.

## The pledge and the witness

Then the verse closes the door on any later denial. They agreed to it, and they were present as witnesses to their own agreement.

The two words are legal in flavour. A later claim of misunderstanding or of never having accepted the terms is ruled out in advance by the record, and the surah uses the record rather than the accusation.

## Why the verse is so short

The verse states the agreement and stops. It does not describe the breach, and the next verse does that with considerable force.

The brevity here makes the next verse possible. A short account of a clear promise set against a detailed account of its violation is an arrangement, and the arrangement is the argument. A reader who has just agreed to something short is in no position to be surprised by a long list of what was done to it.

## In short

- The covenant narrows to blood and homes, the two ways a community damages itself.
- The odd phrasing treats the community as one body, since a member killed is a wound in the whole.
- The pledge and the witness remove any later claim of misunderstanding or non-acceptance.
- The brevity makes the detailed account of the breach in the next verse hit as hard as it does.

## What the verse does

==But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest? Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment? For Allah is never unaware of what you do== is the longest verse in the passage and it produces a single devastating inconsistency.

## The accusation

The verse opens with the words here you are, the tone of a man pointing at something in plain view. Then it lists what is happening. Killing, expelling, and helping one another in it, and that last item turns private acts into a collective position.

## The contradiction

Then comes the detail that breaks the case. When the expelled arrive as captives, these same people pay to ransom them. They will spend money to free a man they drove out and will not simply let him stay.

## Why the ransom was paid

Behind the practice there was a rule they knew. Ransoming captives was commanded and expelling them forbidden, and they kept one and broke the other. A community that obeys a text selectively has not misunderstood it but divided it.

## The question and its force

Then the question about believing part of the book and rejecting part, and it is not answered, since the action has answered it.

The verse shows a people who treated the scripture as a set of options, and the question names what that is. It is not devotion with gaps but a decision about which parts have authority.

## The consequences named

Disgrace is named for this life and a heavier punishment for the next, the two joined in one sentence. What was done in public is answered in public, and what was hidden is answered elsewhere. The closing clause ends the passage as the previous block ended, the same reassurance, repeated because the reader has just seen people behave as though it were untrue.

## In short

- The verse lists killing, expelling, and mutual help, turning private acts into a collective position.
- The contradiction is produced by one detail, that they ransom the people they drove out.
- The arithmetic shows selective obedience rather than misunderstanding, since one rule was kept and the other broken.
- The question names what selective obedience is, and the verse leaves it unanswered because the action answered it.

## What the verse does

==These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped== names the transaction behind everything the passage has described.

## The trade again

Buying and selling has appeared repeatedly, and it appears here for the same purpose. It converts a series of acts into a single exchange, and an exchange can be weighed in a way that a list of acts cannot.

What is named as sold is the Hereafter and what is named as bought is this world. The direction is stated plainly, and the verse does not soften it with adjectives. The reader is left to weigh the two sides of the exchange himself.

## Why the price was accepted

The verse does not say the traders were deceived. It presents a considered exchange, and the reader has just been shown the reasoning that produced it, which makes the exchange look less like a mistake than a decision.

The previous verse described a community keeping the profitable clauses of a covenant. That is the arithmetic of someone who has decided which account matters, and the verse names the decision without arguing against it.

## The two consequences

Then the punishment is described as neither lightened nor shared. Reduction and assistance are the two things a person in difficulty hopes for, and both are refused in a single line that offers no alternative.

The pairing covers the two directions of relief. A sentence can be shortened or someone can be sent to help, and the verse closes both doors with one line.

## What the passage has built

The reader has now been shown a claim to exemption, a rule, a covenant, a breach, and finally a trade, each about the same thing from a different angle.

The verse is where the accounting becomes explicit. Everything before it can be read as the conduct of people who had already decided the exchange rate, and the line states the rate plainly.

## In short

- The market image converts a series of acts into a single exchange, as it has earlier in the surah.
- The trade is presented as considered rather than as a mistake, since the previous verse showed the reasoning.
- Reduction and assistance are refused, closing both directions of relief in one line.
- The verse makes the accounting explicit, so everything before it reads as the conduct of people who had settled the rate.

## What the verse does

==Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others== supplies the history behind the charge and ends on a question.

## The gifts listed

A book is given to one messenger, and messengers follow in succession, and one of them is named with his mother and given clear proofs and support.

The list is a record of generosity, and it is delivered without any commentary on the people who received it. That is what makes the question at the end land as hard as it does, since the reader has been counting gifts and is suddenly asked to account for the response to them.

## The naming of Jesus

He is named as the son of Mary, and the proofs given to him are described as clear. The verse records the honour without disputing anything about him.

That treatment is deliberate in a passage addressed to a people with their own arguments about him. The surah states what was given and leaves the disagreements where they sit.

## The pattern stated

Then the verse names what has happened every time. A messenger arrives with something the people do not like, and the response is arrogance, rejection, and in some cases killing.

The clause something you do not like is the diagnosis. The problem was never the evidence but the content, and the content was disliked before it was examined.

## The question at the end

The verse asks why this keeps happening, and it asks the people directly. The question is not about a single incident but about a habit that has repeated across generations.

That shift from record to question is the shape of the whole passage. The surah has been laying out evidence and here it turns and asks its reader to account for the pattern it has just documented.

## In short

- The gifts are listed without commentary, which is what makes the closing question land.
- The naming of Jesus records the honour given him without entering the disputes about him.
- The phrase something you do not like is the diagnosis, since the objection was to content rather than evidence.
- The move from record to question asks the reader to account for a habit rather than an incident.

## What the verse does

==They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!” In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief. They have but little faith== records their defence and then declines to accept it.

## The defence

The claim is that their hearts are closed, and the wording suggests a covering or a sheath. It is a way of saying that the message cannot get in.

The claim is interesting because it is an admission dressed as an excuse. It concedes that the message has not been accepted and offers a reason that removes responsibility, and the reason is placed in the structure of the heart rather than in the conduct of the person.

## The refusal

The verse answers with a denial, and the denial is blunt. The hearts are not incapable. A curse has fallen because of the disbelief, and the disbelief came first, so the condition being offered as an excuse is in fact the consequence of the thing it was meant to excuse.

So the order is reversed. The condition is not the cause of the refusal. The refusal is the cause of the condition, and the verse says so in one sentence.

## The measure at the end

Then the verse adds a phrase about how little they believe. The wording is a measure, and it is a strange one to apply to people who have just refused everything.

The phrase does two things at once. It denies that the refusal was total and denies that what remains is worth much. A little belief is not nothing and it is not enough, and the verse leaves the reader to hold both of those at the same time.

## Why this is not the last word

The verse is severe and it does not close the passage. The next verses continue the argument, and the continuation is a form of patience.

That is the pattern of the whole section. Each refusal is answered and each answer leaves a door ajar, and the surah keeps the argument going for longer than a reader might expect.

## In short

- The defence concedes the refusal and offers a reason that removes responsibility.
- The verse reverses the order, making the refusal the cause of the condition rather than its result.
- The closing measure denies that the refusal was total and denies that what remains is worth much.
- The verse is severe without being the last word, and the continuing argument is a form of patience.

## What the verse does

==Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists, when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it. So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers== records an expectation and its disappointment in the same sentence.

## The prayer before the event

The verse says they used to ask for victory, and the asking was tied to a coming messenger. They expected to be helped through him, and the expectation was a settled feature of their life rather than a passing hope, which is what makes the reversal so complete.

So the arrival was something they wanted, and the record says they asked for it repeatedly before it happened.

## The recognition

Then the verse says they recognised the book. That word is the hinge of the whole verse, and it removes every defence, because a person who recognises something cannot claim afterwards that he was unable to tell it from something else.

They were not in a position of uncertainty. The text matched what they already held, and they could see the match. The rejection happened after recognition.

## The disappointment

The reversal is complete in a single clause. What they had prayed for arrived and they turned it away, and the verse does not add a word of explanation to that.

The verse does not explain the reason, and it does not need to. A reader who has followed the passage already knows about the price, the position, and the standing that would be lost.

## The closing invocation

The verse ends with a statement of condemnation, and its placement at the end of the sentence gives it the force of a verdict delivered after the evidence rather than before it.

That closing is not the surah speaking in anger but the conclusion the evidence has produced, stated in the form the language uses for a settled judgement.

## In short

- The prayer for victory was tied to a coming messenger, so the arrival was something they had asked for.
- The word recognised removes every defence, since the rejection happened after the match was seen.
- The reversal is complete in one clause, and the reason is left to the reader who already knows the passage.
- The closing condemnation is stated as a settled verdict rather than as an outburst.

## What the verse does

==Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath. And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment== names the motive that the previous verse left out, and the motive is envy.

## The price again

The verse opens by calling the price miserable, and the market image has now been used so often in this passage that the reader knows what it means.

What they sold is named as their own souls. That is the sharpest version of the image yet, because the seller and the goods are the same person.

## Two charges

Then the verse names both what they denied and why. The revelation is denied, and the denial is traced to resentment that favour was given to someone else.

The second charge is the one that explains the first. A person who resents where a gift has landed has a reason to reject the gift, and the verse states the reason without softening it.

## Why envy explains the passage

Everything described in the preceding verses now has a motive attached. The concealment, the selective obedience, and the refusal to recognise all make sense if the underlying objection was to who received the message.

That is a harder charge than unbelief in the abstract. It is the accusation that the argument was never about the evidence.

## Wrath upon wrath

The phrase describes an accumulation, and it fits the history the passage has been recounting. The refusals did not happen once and stop.

Each generation repeated the pattern, and the verse describes the consequence as compounding rather than as a single sentence. What is described is a record, not an incident.

## The humiliation named

The punishment is described as humiliating, and that word connects back to the beginning of the verse. A people worried about their standing are told that the outcome concerns their standing.

The surah does not choose the word at random. The charge was about position and the penalty named is about position, and the fitting is deliberate.

## In short

- The market image reaches its sharpest form, since what was sold is named as the sellers themselves.
- Two charges are made, and the second explains the first, because resentment of where the gift landed gives a reason to reject it.
- Envy supplies the motive that the preceding verses left blank, and it is a harder charge than unbelief in the abstract.
- The punishment is called humiliating because the charge was about standing, and the fitting is deliberate.

## What the verse does

==When it is said to them: “Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,” and they deny what came afterwards, though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before, if you are ˹truly˺ believers?”== stages an offer and a refusal, and the refusal is worded as a principle rather than a preference.

## The terms of the refusal

The invitation is to believe in what Allah has revealed. The answer sets a boundary. They believe in what was sent down to them, and the sentence is arranged so that the boundary sounds like loyalty to a tradition received from the past.

The verse then names what the boundary does in practice. It excludes what came afterwards, and it does so as a single act rather than as a series of small decisions.

## The confirmation they pass over

The excluded message is described as the truth, and as confirming what they already hold. That detail takes away the ordinary reason for refusing a claimant, since a person who trusts a book has a reason to look at a message that agrees with it.

The verse says the agreement was present and the refusal happened anyway. What it is showing is a boundary drawn before the evidence was weighed, and the wording keeps the claim to a revelation next to the refusal of a revelation that matches it.

## The question that closes the case

The verse ends with a question addressed to them about the prophets who were killed before. A claim to believe in what was sent down is being tested against the record of what was done to the people who brought it.

The question is not answered in the verse, and it is not meant to be. Its work is to move the argument from what they say about their book to what their history says about their reception of messengers, and the reader is left holding both.

## In short

- An invitation is answered with a boundary, and the boundary is stated as loyalty to the past rather than as a preference.
- The rejected message is named as the truth that confirms what they already possess, which removes the usual reason for refusal.
- The line was drawn before the evidence was weighed, and the verse keeps the claim and the contradiction side by side.
- A closing question shifts from their description of their book to the record of what was done to earlier messengers.

## What the verse does

==Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully== answers the claim of the previous verse by naming a single event, and it names it without argument.

## The messenger and the proofs

The verse begins with Moses and with what he brought. The proofs are called clear, so the question of whether the message was convincing is settled before the calf is mentioned.

The order matters. A reader might expect a defence of Moses or an account of his mission. The verse gives neither. It states that the case was clear, then moves to what happened next, and the move is quick enough to be the whole argument.

## The interval

The words in his absence mark the time between the departure of the guide and the arrival of the substitute. It is the hour when a people who had been following a person must follow a teaching instead, and the verse places the failure exactly there.

What was set up in that gap was a calf, an object that could be seen and carried about and could be led wherever the people went. The verse does not describe the reasoning behind the choice. It describes the choice, and the silence about the reasoning is itself a judgement on it.

## The verdict

The closing word calls the act wrongful, and that word forecloses a reading of the incident as confusion. They are not described as mistaken or unaware. They are described as people who had been given proofs and had wronged.

The verse is the answer to the question left open just before it. A community that claims to hold what was sent down to it is shown a generation that held it and replaced it, and the replacement happened while the messenger was still close enough to remember. That is the detail the surah wants carried forward.

## In short

- The verse names one event instead of arguing, and the clarity of the proofs is settled before the calf appears.
- The failure is placed in the interval after the guide departs, the hour when a teaching must be followed without a person to follow.
- The object they chose could be seen and carried, and the verse reports the choice rather than the reasoning behind it.
- The closing word rules out confusion, so the incident stands as a wrong done by people who had been shown the way.

## What the verse does

==And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey,” they answered, “We hear and disobey.” The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do, if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!”== goes back to the covenant and reports the sentence the people spoke at the moment of it.

## The mountain held over them

The scene is the covenant taken with the mountain lifted above them, a setting in which the seriousness of the undertaking could not be missed. The command is reported in two parts, hold firmly to what has been given, and obey. Holding firmly is about grip, and obeying is about what the grip is for.

## The answer

What they said is recorded in four words, and the last of them breaks the sentence in half. They heard, and they disobeyed. The verse keeps both halves, because the first is what makes the second a decision rather than an ignorance.

A hearing that ends in refusal is the subject of the verse. It is the plainest form of the argument the surah has been making, since nothing can be added to a person who has already heard.

## What was in the heart

Then the calf, and the verse says it was drunk into their hearts. The image is of something absorbed rather than kept at a distance, a loyalty that had entered the interior and settled there. Their disbelief is named as the reason it went in, and the verse treats the calf as the shape their belief had taken rather than as a lapse of memory.

## The question at the end

The verse closes by asking how evil the thing is that their belief prompts them to do, if belief is what they have. The condition is placed at the end, and it is the sharpest part of the sentence, because it names the fruit as the test of the tree.

## In short

- The covenant is set beneath a raised mountain, and the command joins holding the book firmly to obeying what it says.
- Their answer is quoted in full, and the refusal is joined to a hearing that had already taken place.
- The calf is described as drunk into the hearts, an image of something absorbed rather than kept outside.
- The final question makes their own claim of belief the measure of what they did, and leaves the answer with them.

## What the verse does

==Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!”== proposes a test, and the test is a wish.

## The claim being addressed

The verse is addressed to a claim about the next home. The claim is that the Hereafter belongs to one people among all humanity, an exclusive inheritance rather than a share in a common outcome.

The wording keeps the claim in the mouths of the people making it. The command to speak is given to the Prophet, and what follows is a reply shaped as a challenge rather than a denial.

## Why a wish

A wish for death is an unusual test, and it works because it costs the person making the claim something he cannot take back. Anyone convinced that the next life is his alone has nothing to fear from the door that leads to it.

The verse does not ask for a proof, an argument, or a document. It asks for a desire, and a desire cannot be produced on request if it is not there. That is why the test is fair. It asks the claimants to put their own confidence where their sentence already placed it.

## The condition attached

The challenge closes with a condition. If what they say is true, the wish should follow, and the verse leaves the two tied together in one sentence.

That structure puts the claim and the test in the same breath, so a refusal to wish becomes a statement about the claim. The reader is not asked to judge the claim directly. The reader is shown what the claim would produce in a person who actually held it, and the producing is the argument.

A claim about the unseen is hard to test from outside. A claim held by someone who is willing to stake his remaining days on it is a different matter, and the verse arranges for that stake to be visible without requiring anyone to prove anything.

## In short

- The verse answers an exclusive claim about the next home with a test rather than with a denial.
- The test is a wish for death, which costs the person who makes it something that cannot be recovered.
- A desire cannot be summoned on request, so the absence of the wish answers the claim by itself.
- Claim and test stand in one sentence, and the reader draws the conclusion from the silence that follows.

## What the verse does

==But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers== answers the challenge of the verse before it, and it answers before the challenge is taken up.

## The refusal stated in advance

The verse says they will never wish for it. The certainty is not a forecast about a future event so much as a statement about something already visible in them, and the reason is supplied in the same breath.

A challenge usually waits for a response. This one is answered by the text itself, which removes the possibility that the refusal will be read as an accident or a passing mood, and it puts the verdict in the same voice that issued the challenge.

## What their hands have done

The reason given is what their hands have done, a phrase that covers everything a person earns and sends ahead. It is the surah's usual way of naming deeds, and it keeps the responsibility attached to the one who acted.

What they have done is not described in detail, because the verse is not interested in the list. It is interested in the effect, which is a person who does not want to be told what the next life holds for him.

## The knowledge at the end

The closing clause says that Allah has perfect knowledge of the wrongdoers, and it does two things at once. It says the refusal is seen, and it says the reason for it is known.

The word for wrongdoers is the one used in the previous passage for a similar act. The verse is not bringing a new accusation but showing that the same thing is still being done under a different description, and the repetition of the word is how the reader is meant to notice it.

## In short

- The challenge is answered by the text before it is taken up, so the refusal cannot be read as a mood or an accident.
- The reason is what their hands have done, a phrase that keeps responsibility attached to the person who acted.
- The deeds are left unnamed because the effect is what matters, and the effect is a person who does not want to know the outcome.
- The closing clause joins the refusal to a knowledge that sees it, and repeats the word for wrongdoing used earlier.

## What the verse does

==You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years. But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do== turns from the refusal of death to the appetite for life that produces it.

## The measure doubled

The verse says they cling to life more eagerly than any other people, and then adds a second comparison that goes further, more than those who associate partners with Allah.

The measure is doubled because the claim being tested was a claim of privilege. A people who call themselves heirs of the next life are shown clutching this one hardest.

## The thousand years

Each of them wishes to live a thousand years, and the number is not a calculation. It is the shape of a wish that has no natural stopping point, since a person who wants a thousand would accept more.

The verse does not present the wish as a plan. It presents it as a disposition, and a disposition shows itself in the number a person chooses when nothing limits him. A thousand is what a man says when he is not counting, and the verse reports the figure as evidence of appetite, not news about the man.

## The answer to the wish

Then the verse says that a long life would not save them from the punishment. The wish is granted in imagination and it still fails, which takes away the last shelter a person might look for.

The sentence turns appetite into a confession. A person who wants more time is a person who has not found a reason to be ready, and the verse gives him that time as a supposition, so the failure is visible before anyone lives through it.

## The last clause

The verse ends with the statement that Allah sees what they do. The seeing is placed after the appetite because appetite is what the verse has been describing, and the reader is left with the two facts together.

## In short

- The appetite for life is measured twice, first against all people and then against those who associate others with Allah.
- The thousand years is not a calculation but the shape of a wish with no stopping point.
- The wish is granted in imagination and still fails, which removes the last shelter a person might look for.
- The closing clause places the appetite under a seeing that misses nothing, and leaves the two facts side by side.

## What the verse does

==Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.”== answers an objection about the angel who brought the revelation.

## The objection behind the verse

The verse opens with a condition about enmity toward Gabriel, and the condition is the answer to an argument that is never quoted. What is quoted is the conclusion, and the reader is told what follows from it.

The surah has been dealing with people who set conditions on what they will accept. Here the condition has moved from the content of the message to the person who carried it.

## Who brought it

The verse says Gabriel revealed it to your heart, and the phrase does two things. It names the carrier as one who acted by Allah's will, and it names the place the message reached, which is the interior of the recipient rather than a page.

Enmity toward the carrier is therefore answered by describing what the carrier did. A servant who brings a gift is not the author of the gift, and the verse keeps the two roles apart, so that the quarrel is seen for what it is before it is answered at all.

## What the message is said to be

Four descriptions follow. It confirms what came before it, it is a guide, it is good news, and it is for the believers. The first matters for the argument, because a message that agrees with what a people already hold cannot be dismissed as a foreign arrival.

The other three describe what the message does for the people who take it. Guide and good news are placed together, so that the direction and the comfort are one act. The verse closes on the people who receive it, not on the ones who refused it, and the last word of the sentence is the one that names them.

## In short

- The verse answers an objection that is never quoted, and answers it by describing the carrier rather than the objection.
- Gabriel is named as one who acted by Allah's will, and the message is said to have reached the heart of the recipient.
- The message is described as confirming what came before, which takes away the charge that it is an alien arrival.
- Guide and good news are named together, so that direction and comfort are presented as one act.

## What the verse does

==Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers== widens the condition of the verse before it until it covers everything a person might set himself against.

## The list

The verse names Allah, then His angels, then His messengers, then two angels by name. The order moves from the source to the servants, and the two names at the end are the ones that had been made a subject of dispute.

A list of this shape is not a catalogue. It is a way of saying that the order is one order, and that a person cannot take one part of it as an ally while treating another part as an enemy.

## Why the two names

Gabriel and Michael are mentioned after the general term for angels, which means the general term was not enough for the argument being made. The two were singled out because the objection being answered had singled them out.

The verse is telling the reader that hostility does not survive contact with a list. What looked like a preference about one carrier turns out to be a position about the whole arrangement, and the arrangement is not divisible into parts that can be accepted or refused separately.

## The conclusion

What follows is stated in the plural, and the plural is deliberate. The verse does not say that Allah is the enemy of the one who is hostile. It says that Allah is the enemy of the disbelievers, so the hostility is classified before it is answered.

That classification is the harshest thing in the verse. A person may imagine that he is quarrelling with a servant. The verse says he has placed himself outside a relation that the servants only carry, and the carrying is what he was objecting to in the first place.

## In short

- The verse widens a narrow objection until it covers the whole order of Allah, His angels, and His messengers.
- Two angels are named after the general term because the objection had named them, so the reply meets the argument where it was made.
- Hostility that picks one carrier is shown to be a position about the whole arrangement rather than a preference.
- The conclusion stands in the plural, which classifies the hostility before answering it and is the harshest line in the verse.

## What the verse does

==Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious== is short, and it makes two claims that answer each other.

## The clarity of what was sent

The first claim concerns the revelation itself. It is described as clear, and the clarity is not a quality that depends on the reader. The verses are said to carry their own evidence, and the statement is made by the One who sent them.

That claim matters because the surah has been reporting refusals, and a reader could reasonably ask whether the refusals were caused by weakness in what was presented. The verse removes that explanation in its first sentence, and it removes it before the reader has time to construct it.

The verses are also said to have been sent down to the Prophet, which places the recipient in the same relation to them as any reader who comes later. What was given to him is what has reached the reader, and neither stands outside the clarity being described.

## The character of the denier

The second claim concerns the people who deny. The verse says that none deny them except the rebellious, and it uses a word for someone who has left the boundary.

The word does not describe an intellectual position. It describes a condition of the person, and by placing it here the verse moves the cause of denial from the message to the one who hears it.

## What the two claims do together

Set side by side, the claims leave no middle ground. If the verses are clear and the deniers are the ones who have broken away, then the denial is a fact about them rather than a verdict on what was sent.

The verse does not develop the point. It states it, and the brevity is part of the force, because a short sentence cannot be argued with at length. There is nothing in it to take hold of except its two claims, and both of them are about the same event reported from the side of the sender.

## In short

- The clarity of the revelation is asserted first, so that weakness in the message cannot explain the refusals reported before it.
- Denial is then traced to a condition in the person, named with a word for one who has left the boundary.
- Placed together, the claims leave no middle ground between a clear message and a hearer who has broken away.
- The verse states rather than argues, and the brevity keeps the matter from turning into a discussion.

## What the verse does

==Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe== asks a question about a pattern, and the pattern is what makes it a question rather than a report.

## Every time

The verse begins with a question about frequency. It is not asking whether a covenant was broken but why the same thing keeps happening, and the repetition is the evidence.

A single breach can be explained by weakness, inattention, or circumstance. A breach that recurs at every covenant removes those explanations and leaves something that belongs to the people themselves, and the question is shaped to make the reader notice which explanation is left standing.

The question is also gentle in its grammar. It asks why rather than declaring that, and the asking gives the accused a moment to answer before the verse answers for them.

## A group of them

The verse does not say that all of them broke it. It says that a group among them cast it aside, and the wording is precise. A group is enough to break a covenant made by a community, and the verse does not let the others off by counting them.

The casting aside is the same image used elsewhere in the surah for a book put behind the back. What is thrown away is not lost. It is placed where the thrower will not have to look at it.

## The correction

Then the verse corrects its own question. Most of them do not believe. The acts of breaking are the visible surface, and the sentence goes underneath it to name the root.

That movement from conduct to belief is the pattern of the whole passage. The surah keeps showing what people do and then naming what lies at the bottom of it, and here the naming is compressed into a single clause at the end of a question.
